newsitem.title: UK: Romania seeks deeper reform, faster privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Romania seeks deeper reform, faster privatisation.

text.p: Romania will step up its privatisation process and restructure key sectors of the economy as part of broad reforms agreed with international lenders, senior officials said.

State secretary at the finance ministry Ionut Mircea Costea, speaking at a weekend meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), said Romania was striving to build credibility with international investors.
"The new policy involves further improvement of the legal framework to make Romania more attractive for foreign investors," he said.
Daniel Daianu, chief economist at the central bank, said privatisation of state banks was a main plank of the reforms.

Earlier this month, the government rushed to approve a long-awaited bill on bank privatisation before the arrival of an International Monetary Fund (IMF) delegation. The draft law is now awaiting approval by parliament.
"There is going to be much better supervision of banks," Daianu said. "We are determined to do it. We are going to speed up privatistion of banks."
Government sources say Romania is seeking about $400 million in credits from the IMF and up to $600 million from the World Bank.

Bogdan Baltazar, vice-president of Romania's State Ownership Fund, which is responsible for privatisation, said forthcoming sell-offs included a helicopter manufacturer, a major electrical goods firm, a big cement plant and oil refineries.
"A couple of refineries will be put to bid very shortly," Baltazar said, adding that the government was considering restructuring the entire energy sector.
"There is an idea to have a national oil company, but a competitive one," he said.
He described the present state oil conglomerate as "an old lady or gentleman who has performed a function and should be thanked".
"We will probably keep the national oil corporation that is doing the extraction and pumping, keep two big refineries and all the gas stations that are left," he said.
About 60 percent of Romania's petrol stations are in private hands and most of those are foreign owned.
Baltazar said the crude oil and refined oil product transport firms would be separate entities under a regulatory authority.
